title: Śrīdhara Svāmī literal English — Canto 4, chapter 1, second checkpoint
source_alignment: The pinned Sanskrit has two successive headings marked 4.1.31. The first corresponds to English 31 and the second to English 32. Subsequent Sanskrit headings 32–61 correspond to English verse number plus one; the Sanskrit heading jumps from 61 to 63, where the numbering realigns. Several source verse blocks straddle English verse breaks (especially English 46–55); glosses below are keyed by the Sanskrit words they actually interpret rather than the defective heading alone. Verse numbers in the English mirror were individually cross-checked against the Sanskrit verse text.

entries.text: ‘They will spread’ means ‘they will extend.’ It is a form of the root sṛp, ‘to move,’ with a causative sense included in it.
Having been properly honored, that is, worshipped, by the two of them, they departed from that place.
Aṅgiras was Brahmā's third son. ‘Understand’ means ‘know.’
He names those daughters with ‘Sinīvālī’ and the following names.
The construction is: Pulastya [begot them] in his wife Havirbhū. ‘He’ is Agastya. Dahra-agni is the digestive fire. ‘And Viśravā’ means that Viśravā too was a son of Pulastya.
Kubera was the son born to Viśravā in Iḍaviḍā. Rāvaṇa and the other two sons were born to his other wife, Keśinī.
‘Blazing’ means ‘shining.’
They were born with Citraketu at their head, and they became the seven seers.
He names those very ones with ‘Citraketu.’ Vasubhṛdyāna is the name of a single person. Those others beginning with Śakti are sons of another [wife].
[He begot them] in his wife Khyāti. ‘Sons’ includes two sons and one daughter; he names them with ‘Dhātā’ and so forth.
‘Of the two’ means of Dhātā and Vidhātā.
Kavi the Bhārgava is a son of Bhṛgu; Uśanā is the son of that Kavi.
‘Son of the Unborn’ means a son of Brahmā, not the later Dakṣa descended from the Pracetas.
‘To the united ones’ means to those who are restrained, or alternatively to those who are assembled.
She is the one in whom all the qualities have their origin.
‘They attended upon [them]’ means ‘they worshipped [them].’

In that Self, by His own māyā, this universe is fashioned like a city of the Gandharvas, an appearance of forms in the sky. To make that Self manifest, He today manifested Himself; obeisance to that Person. In what form did He manifest? In a form whose shape is that of a sage.

May He look upon us, the host of gods, with a gaze endowed with abundant compassion, with an extraordinary eye. Of what kind is that gaze? It surpasses the spotless lotus which is the abode of Śrī. Of what kind is He? His reality is to be inferred and considered from scripture, not directly perceived by us. Of what kind are we? Created through the quality of sattva to quiet the disturbance, the alteration of the established order of the world.
Praised by those hosts of gods who had obtained His glance, and worshipped by them, the two departed.

‘For the removal of the burden of the earth’ means for its destruction. The word ‘and’ links the sentence into a single statement: those two have also now come here. Thus it is said in the Tantra: ‘Nara entered Arjuna; Kṛṣṇa is Nārāyaṇa Himself.’ The foremost of the Yadus is Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the foremost of the Kurus is Arjuna. Both bear the name Kṛṣṇa.
They are the deities presiding over fire. Svāhā is his wife. ‘Eaters of oblations’ qualifies all three.
The fathers are three, and the grandfather is one; together with them means along with them.

‘In the vaitānika rite’ means in a Vedic rite. These are the fires in whose names sacrificial offerings to fire-deities are prescribed and performed in sacrifice; they are not ordinary fires. Thus their large number is not without purpose: this is the sense.
‘Saumyas’ means drinkers of soma. Those for whom a rite is performed in fire are ‘with fire’; those lacking that are ‘without fire.’
There were no descendants of those two, because they were liberated while still living; he expresses this with ‘both of them.’
Even though Satī faithfully followed the god who was her equal in qualities and character, she did not obtain a son.

Here is the reason: her own father Dakṣa was unsuitable, that is, opposed to [Śiva]. ‘By herself she abandoned herself’ means that she herself abandoned her body. ‘Joined with yoga’ means having resorted to yoga.
